## Findings

- **At the border, US buyers paid nearly all of the 2025–26 tariffs.** Prices charged by foreign
  exporters before duty barely moved when tariffs rose: the estimated response is
  `{python} N["b25"]` (SE `{python} N["b25_se"]`), and `{python} N["b25_t3"]` with outliers
  trimmed, where 0 means the duty was added in full to what US importers paid and −1 means
  exporters cut their prices by the full duty. Of each dollar of duty, roughly
  `{python} N["buyer_lo"]` to `{python} N["buyer_hi"]` cents fell on US buyers. That is the same
  result the 2018–19 trade war produced, and we reproduce it with the same data and method
  (`{python} N["b18"]`; `{python} N["b18_t3"]` trimmed).
- **Section 232 metals and autos are the one place exporters gave a little.** Their estimate is
  `{python} N["s23225"]` in 2025–26 (`{python} N["s232_18"]` in 2018–19). BLS import price indexes
  by country of origin, measured before duty, agree: `{python} N["mxp25"]` (SE
  `{python} N["mxp25_se"]`).
- **In stores, prices of exposed goods rose by part of the duty cost, gradually.** Measured
  against each item's own pre-2025 trend, consumer prices rose by about `{python} N["th_main"]`
  (statutory exposure) to `{python} N["th_eff"]` (duties collected) of the duty cost of the
  item's imports, about `{python} N["th_main_ratio"]`–`{python} N["th_eff_ratio"]` of the border
  response. These estimates are imprecise; none is statistically significant at conventional levels.
- **Tariffs collected were well below the rates on paper.** The effective rate (duties assessed
  ÷ imports) peaked at `{python} N["eff_peak"]` in `{python} N["eff_peak_month"]` against a
  statutory rate of `{python} N["stat_peak"]`, because of USMCA claims, in-transit exemptions and
  duties on metal content only. It was `{python} N["eff_last"]` in `{python} N["data_month"]`,
  after the Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs.
- **Trade moved away from China.** China's share of US imports of the products tariffed in
  2018–19 fell from `{python} N["sh_s301_cn0"]` to `{python} N["sh_s301_cn24"]` by 2024 and
  `{python} N["sh_s301_cn1"]` in the year to `{python} N["div_last"]`; Taiwan, Vietnam, Mexico and
  other Southeast Asian suppliers grew. In a gravity model the elasticity of imports to tariffs
  is `{python} N["dv_ppml25"]` (`{python} N["dv_ppml18"]` in 2018–19).
- **Importers stockpiled before each action, then cut back.** Imports of goods facing the China,
  metals and reciprocal tariffs ran above their own trend for `{python} N["fr_months_lo"]`–`{python} N["fr_months_hi"]`
  months before the duties, by `{python} N["fr_excess"]` in all, and fell below it afterwards.

The [product explorer](explore.qmd) shows the tariff rates, prices and import sources behind
these estimates for any HS10 product.

## Data and tariff timeline

The analysis uses public data only:

| Source | What it gives | Level |
|---|---|---|
| Census international trade API [@census_trade] | Imports for consumption: customs value, quantity, calculated duties | HS10 product × country × month |
| Tariff timeline (this project) [@federal_register] | Every tariff action, rate, HS scope, dates, legal status, with citations | Action component |
| BLS CPI [@bls_cpi] | Consumer price indexes, detailed items | Item × month |
| BLS import price indexes [@bls_mxp] | Import prices by country of origin, before duty | Locality × month |
| BEA input-output tables [@bea_io] | Import share of supply; PCE bridge to consumer categories | Commodity |
| Treasury Monthly Treasury Statement [@treasury_mts] | Customs receipts (reconciliation) | Month |

Monthly import totals reconcile to the published FT-900 within tolerance and calculated duties to
Treasury customs receipts after timing lags (details in
[DATA.md](https://github.com/johnpospisil/tariff-pass-through/blob/main/DATA.md)).

**The tariff timeline** is the core of the project: `{python} N["tl_rows"]` action components in
`{python} N["tl_groups"]` actions, from the 2018 Section 201 safeguards to the 2026 Section 232 and
Section 301 actions. Each component carries an official source (Federal Register citation,
proclamation or executive order number, USTR notice or CBP message) and the date it was verified.
The timeline is expanded to a rate for every HS10 product × country × month, applying the stacking
rules in the orders, exclusions and USMCA treatment.


## Effective tariff rates

```{python}
#| output: asis
print(nm.fig("chart2_effective_rates", "Statutory and effective tariff rates by trading partner"))
```

The average effective tariff rate on US imports was `{python} N["eff_2024"]` in 2024. It rose
with the 2025 actions to a peak of `{python} N["eff_peak"]` in `{python} N["eff_peak_month"]` and
was `{python} N["eff_last"]` in `{python} N["data_month"]` (Penn Wharton Budget Model, on a
slightly different import base: `{python} N["pwbm_eff"]` [@pwbm2026]). For China the effective
rate peaked at `{python} N["eff_cn_peak"]` in `{python} N["eff_cn_peak_month"]` and was
`{python} N["eff_cn_last"]` in `{python} N["data_month"]` (Penn Wharton: `{python} N["pwbm_cn_eff"]`).

The statutory rate, what the orders say applies, ran well above duties actually assessed:
`{python} N["stat_peak"]` at its peak, and `{python} N["stat_cn_peak"]` for China in April 2025,
when most goods shipped before the increase were still exempt in transit. The gap comes from
identifiable sources: USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico enter free (Canada
`{python} N["eff_ca_last"]` effective against `{python} N["stat_ca_last"]` statutory; Mexico
`{python} N["eff_mx_last"]` against `{python} N["stat_mx_last"]`), Section 232 derivative duties fall
on the metal content only, and in-transit exemptions delay each increase by one to two months. We
use the statutory rate as the tariff change in the regressions (it is not affected by importers'
responses) and the rate actually collected as a check.

## Border pass-through

The chart at the top of the page shows the estimates in this section. The question is whether the price a foreign exporter charges, before duty, falls when the tariff
rises. We follow @arw2019: for each product (HS10) and country, the 12-month change in the log
unit value (customs value ÷ quantity) is regressed on the change in ln(1 + tariff), with fixed
effects for HS6 product × month and country × month, so the estimate compares varieties of the
same product in the same month that faced different tariff changes. Standard errors are clustered
by HS8.

- **2025–26** (January 2024 to `{python} N["data_month"]`): `{python} N["b25"]`
  (SE `{python} N["b25_se"]`); `{python} N["b25_t3"]` (SE `{python} N["b25_t3_se"]`) when
  varieties whose unit value changed more than threefold are dropped; `{python} N["b25_pre"]`
  ending before the IEEPA ruling. US importers' duty-inclusive prices rose by
  `{python} N["dut_iv25"]` per unit of duty actually collected (instrumenting collected duties with
  statutory rates), and quantities fell by `{python} N["qty_iv25"]`.
- **2018–19**, the same design on the trade war: `{python} N["b18"]` (SE `{python} N["b18_se"]`),
  `{python} N["b18_t3"]` trimmed. @arw2019 report `{python} N["arw_pub"]` and @fgkk2020
  `{python} N["fgkk_pub"]`; our versions of their exact specifications give `{python} N["arw_ours"]`
  and `{python} N["fgkk_ours"]` (the gap is documented in DATA.md). All agree that exporters
  absorbed little of the tariff.
- **By authority** (2025–26): Section 232 `{python} N["s23225"]`; IEEPA `{python} N["ieepa25"]`
  (`{python} N["ieepa25_t3"]` trimmed). **By supplier**: China `{python} N["cn25_t3"]` trimmed.
- **Timing**: in an event study around each variety's first tariff increase, duty-inclusive
  prices jump about `{python} N["ev_dut0"]` in the month the duty applies while pre-duty prices do
  not fall; quantities in the months before sit `{python} N["ev_qty_front"]` below the month just
  before the duty (stockpiling) and fall `{python} N["ev_qty0"]` on impact.
- **Independent check**: BLS import price indexes by country of origin, measured before duty,
  show the same: `{python} N["mxp25"]` (SE `{python} N["mxp25_se"]`) against the tariff on each
  origin's imports.

## At the store: retail prices

```{python}
#| output: asis
print(nm.fig("chart3_retail", "Consumer prices of high- and low-exposure goods"))
```

Each CPI item gets a tariff exposure: the import share of what consumers buy (from BEA's 2017
supply table, through the PCE bridge and BLS's PCE–CPI mapping) times the import-weighted tariff
change. Exposure is the duty as a share of the consumer price if it were passed on in full. The
most exposed items are household appliances (`{python} N["exp_top_name"]`:
`{python} N["exp_top"]`, `{python} N["exp_top_eff"]` on duties collected), apparel, footwear and
consumer electronics; food, fuels and drugs have little exposure.

```{python}
#| output: asis
print(nm.table_exposure())
```

: Most exposed CPI goods items, 2025–26 (window means). {#tbl-exposure}

**Pre-trends matter.** Highly exposed goods were getting cheaper relative to less exposed goods
before 2025: in January 2023 the high-exposure third stood `{python} N["hl_pre_gap"]` index points
above the low third, both indexed to January 2025 (left panel). A comparison that ignores this
reads the end of that decline as a fall in prices (`{python} N["th_notrend"]`). We therefore
measure each item against its own 2023–24 trend (right panel).

On that basis, across `{python} N["th_items"]` CPI goods items in `{python} N["th_classes"]`
expenditure classes, retail prices rose by `{python} N["th_main"]` (SE `{python} N["th_main_se"]`)
of the duty cost on statutory exposure and `{python} N["th_eff"]` (SE `{python} N["th_eff_se"]`)
on duties collected. Compared with the border, where importers' costs rose by about the full duty,
that is `{python} N["th_main_ratio"]` and `{python} N["th_eff_ratio"]` of the border response.
The most exposed third of items rose `{python} N["th_bin"]` (SE `{python} N["th_bin_se"]`)
relative to the least exposed; the gap built up gradually (`{python} N["rev_6"]` six months in,
`{python} N["rev_12"]` after a year) and had not reversed by `{python} N["hl_month"]` despite the
IEEPA ruling (`{python} N["hl_high"]` vs `{python} N["hl_low"]` relative to trend). In 2018–19,
when exposure was far smaller, the same design is too imprecise to say much
(`{python} N["th18"]`, SE `{python} N["th18_se"]`); @cgnt2021 found limited pass-through to
store prices in that episode.


## Trade diversion

```{python}
#| output: asis
print(nm.fig("chart4_diversion", "Supplier shares of US imports"))
```

For products tariffed on China in 2018–19 (`{python} N["s301_value"]` of imports in the year to
`{python} N["div_last"]`), China's share fell from `{python} N["sh_s301_cn0"]` to
`{python} N["sh_s301_cn24"]` by 2024 and `{python} N["sh_s301_cn1"]` by `{python} N["div_last"]`.
Taiwan went from `{python} N["sh_s301_tw0"]` to `{python} N["sh_s301_tw1"]` (mostly computers and
servers), Vietnam from `{python} N["sh_s301_vn0"]` to `{python} N["sh_s301_vn1"]`, Mexico from
`{python} N["sh_s301_mx0"]` to `{python} N["sh_s301_mx1"]` and other Southeast Asia from
`{python} N["sh_s301_sea0"]` to `{python} N["sh_s301_sea1"]`. In all other products China's share
fell from `{python} N["sh_other_cn0"]` to `{python} N["sh_other_cn1"]`, mostly in 2025.

Weighted by trade, imports fell with tariffs in both episodes: a gravity model (PPML, HS6 ×
quarter and HS6 × country fixed effects) gives `{python} N["dv_ppml25"]` for 2025–26 and
`{python} N["dv_ppml18"]` for 2018–19. One unweighted comparison in 2025–26 gives the opposite
sign (`{python} N["dv_ld25"]`): within a product, the mid-tariff suppliers that replaced China
(Vietnam, Thailand) grew while facing larger increases than Canada and Mexico. It measures
substitution toward China's competitors, not the response to a supplier's own tariff; China's
own coefficient is `{python} N["dv_ldcn25"]`.

```{python}
#| output: asis
print(nm.table_diversion())
```

: Response of imports to Δln(1 + tariff), coefficient (SE), clustered by HS6. {#tbl-diversion}

**Possible transshipment.** We list products where China's share fell by at least `{python} N["fl_cn_drop"]` points
while a supplier with under `{python} N["fl_prior"]` before reached at least
`{python} N["fl_post"]` and gained at least `{python} N["fl_gain"]` a year, with whether
its unit values moved toward China's. From 2017 to 2024: `{python} N["fl_a_n"]` such cases,
`{python} N["fl_a_bn"]` of gains, `{python} N["fl_a_conv"]` with converging unit values. From 2024
to the latest year: `{python} N["fl_b_n"]` cases, `{python} N["fl_b_bn"]`,
`{python} N["fl_b_conv"]` converging. These patterns are consistent with rerouting and equally with
production genuinely moving; they are a list of where to look, not evidence of evasion.

## Front-running

```{python}
#| output: asis
print(nm.fig("chart5_front_running", "Imports of affected products around the 2025 actions"))
```

For each 2025 action we compare imports of the affected product × country pairs with their own
seasonal pattern and pre-election growth. Goods facing the China, metals and reciprocal tariffs ran
above trend for `{python} N["fr_months_lo"]`–`{python} N["fr_months_hi"]` months, peaking in the
month before the duty, with `{python} N["fr_excess"]` of excess imports. The largest single surge
was pharmaceuticals (`{python} N["fr_pharma_peak"]` in March 2025) when the Section 232 inquiry
opened. Afterwards imports fell below trend. Months around each effective date are excluded or
tested separately in the pass-through estimates.

## De minimis

```{python}
#| output: asis
print(nm.fig("chart6_low_value", "Recorded low-value imports"))
```

Duty-free entry for shipments under `{python} N["dm_threshold"]` ended for China and Hong Kong in May 2025 and for all
countries in August 2025. Those shipments were not in Census trade data before
(`{python} N["dm_2023"]` in 2023, about `{python} N["dm_month"]` a month, by @fk2025's estimate).
Census records low-value formal entries under a single estimate line [@census_guide]; for China and
Hong Kong it went from about `{python} N["lv_cn_pre"]` a month in early 2025 to
`{python} N["lv_cn_last"]` in `{python} N["data_month"]`, and for other countries from
`{python} N["lv_rest_pre"]` to `{python} N["lv_rest_last"]`. **Part of that rise is a change in
measurement**: trade that used to enter unrecorded now appears. The recorded increase is far smaller
than the former de minimis flow, so most of that trade either stopped or is still not visible in
this line.

## Robustness

```{python}
#| output: asis
print(nm.fig("chart_spec_curve", "Specification curve"))
```

We re-estimated the border coefficient `{python} N["rb_fits"]` ways: `{python} N["rb_rules"]` rules
for cleaning unit values, alternative fixed effects and clustering, dropping China or Section 232 products, excluding
front-running months, single years and the pre-ruling window. Across the `{python} N["rb_n"]`
unweighted 2025–26 specifications the estimate lies between `{python} N["rb_lo"]` and
`{python} N["rb_hi"]`, and no confidence interval goes below `{python} N["rb_ci_lo"]`. Weighting by import
value gives `{python} N["rb_weighted"]`, driven by one chapter (computers and servers, whose
product mix shifted toward Taiwan and Mexico), not by exporters cutting prices.

## Limitations

- **Unit values are not prices.** Customs value ÷ quantity mixes price changes with changes in
  what is shipped within a code. We clean outliers, compare within HS6 × month, and check against
  BLS import price indexes, but composition changes remain.
- **Statutory rates overstate duties for some goods.** Section 232 derivative duties apply to metal
  content only and USMCA claims rose in 2025; coefficients on statutory rates are attenuated for
  duty-inclusive prices and quantities, so we also report responses per unit of duty collected.
- **The retail mapping is coarse.** Import shares come from 2017 input-output tables, and many CPI
  items share one PCE bridge line. A hand-mapped route for `{python} N["hand_items"]` major goods gives similar answers.
- **The retail estimates are imprecise** and depend on extrapolating each item's 2023–24 trend.
- **Revisions and gaps.** Census revises recent months (annual revision each June); BLS collected
  no prices for most items in October 2025 (federal shutdown), which we leave missing.
- **Refunds.** Census duties are as assessed at entry; the IEEPA refunds paid in 2026 are a later
  transfer to importers and are not netted out.

## What we don't claim

- **No welfare conclusions.** We measure prices and trade flows. Who ultimately bears a tariff
  also depends on wages, profits, exchange rates and government revenue, which we do not model.
- **No verdict on the policy.** The results describe what happened to prices and trade; they are
  not an assessment of whether the tariffs were good or bad policy.
- **No findings of evasion.** Transshipment flags are statistical patterns.
- **No forecast.** Tariff policy changed several times during the sample and may change again.

## Methods appendix

**Data build.** Census imports for consumption by HS10 × individual country × month from January
2017, cached with a manifest of every request. HS10 codes are linked across years into families
(in the spirit of @pierce_schott2012). Calculated duties reconcile to Treasury customs receipts
after timing; import totals to the FT-900.

**Tariff rates.** Each action in the timeline is expanded to a daily rate by HS10 × country,
applying the stacking rules in the orders (for example, Section 232 duties replace the reciprocal
duty on the same goods), exclusions and USMCA treatment (approximated with the share of each
product's imports claiming USMCA), then averaged over days in the month.

**Border pass-through.** Δ₁₂ ln(unit value) = β Δ₁₂ ln(1 + τ) + HS6 × month + country × month
fixed effects, by HS10 × country variety; also duty-inclusive unit value (unit value × (1 + τ)),
quantity and value; 12-month log changes winsorised at the 1st and 99th percentiles. Heterogeneity
by supplier, tariff authority, differentiated vs homogeneous goods [@rauch1999] and time since the
tariff; event studies following @fgkk2020.

**Retail.** ln CPI = θ × exposure + item + month fixed effects, on log indexes net of item seasonal
factors (2015–24) and each item's linear trend over the pre-period, clustered by expenditure class.
Robustness: 12-month differences, BLS seasonally adjusted series, all items, hand-mapped items,
the pre-ruling window, and a trend fitted from 2015.

**Diversion.** Long differences of import value and share by HS6 × country between seasonally
matched windows two years apart, with HS6 fixed effects; quarterly PPML gravity with HS6 × quarter
and HS6 × country (and country × quarter) fixed effects.

Every estimate is produced by `make` from public data, pinned in tests, and listed in
[DATA.md](https://github.com/johnpospisil/tariff-pass-through/blob/main/DATA.md) with its
specification.

## Data as of and legal status

Trade, tariff and price data run to `{python} N["data_month"]`. The Supreme Court held on
`{python} N["date_ruling"]` that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act does not authorize
tariffs, and IEEPA duties stopped on `{python} N["date_collection_ended"]`. Customs and Border
Protection estimated `{python} N["refunds_assessed"]` of IEEPA duties collected, and had certified
`{python} N["refunds_paid"]` in refunds by `{python} N["refunds_paid_date"]`; the Court of
International Trade certified a nationwide class of importers on `{python} N["date_cit_class"]`.
Status checked on `{python} N["legal_checked"]`.
